content: A keloid is a type of scar that forms due to an excessive growth of fibrous tissue at the site of a healed skin injury. These scars are typically firm and rubbery in texture, or they may appear as shiny, fibrous nodules. Their color can range from pink to flesh-colored, or from red to dark brown. Keloid scars are benign and non-contagious, but they are often associated with significant itching, sharp pain, and changes in skin texture. In severe cases, keloids can impair skin movement. Keloids are distinct from hypertrophic scars, which are raised scars that remain confined to the boundaries of the original wound and may diminish over time. In contrast, keloids can grow beyond the original wound site, expanding in claw-like patterns over normal skin. They may cause needle-like pain or itching without warning, though the intensity of these sensations varies among individuals. If a keloid becomes infected, it may ulcerate. The only definitive treatment is surgical removal, but there is a high likelihood—greater than 50%—that the resulting surgical scar will also develop into a keloid. Keloids form within scar tissue due to an overproduction of collagen, which is a protein involved in wound repair. This overgrowth can result in a lump that is significantly larger than the original scar. While keloids typically develop at the site of an injury, they can also arise spontaneously. They may occur at the site of piercings, pimples, scratches, or even minor skin trauma. Severe acne, chickenpox scarring, wound infections, repeated trauma to an area, excessive skin tension during wound closure, or the presence of a foreign body in a wound can all contribute to keloid formation. In some cases, keloids may be sensitive to chlorine. Keloids affect both sexes equally, but they are more commonly reported in young women, likely due to the higher frequency of earlobe piercings among females. Individuals with darker skin tones, particularly those of African descent, are at a significantly higher risk of developing keloids, with an incidence rate up to 15 times greater than in lighter-skinned populations. Historically, keloids were first described by Egyptian surgeons around 1700 BC. In 1806, Baron Jean-Louis Alibert identified keloids as a distinct entity, initially naming them cancroide before changing the term to cheloide to avoid confusion with cancer. The term keloid is derived from the Greek word chele, meaning crab's claw, and the suffix -oid, meaning resembling. In some cultures, keloid formation has been intentionally induced for decorative or ritualistic purposes. For example, the Olmec civilization in pre-Columbian Mexico used keloid scarification as a form of body decoration. In modern times, women of the Nubia-Kush region in Sudan intentionally create facial keloids for aesthetic purposes. Similarly, the Nuer and Nuba peoples use keloid tattoos on the forehead, chin, and above the lips as part of their cultural practices. In Papua New Guinea, tribal rituals involve cutting the skin and inserting clay or ash into the wounds to create permanent keloid-like bumps, which are seen as symbols of courage and endurance. Keloids are most commonly found on the earlobes, sternum, shoulders, upper back, and other areas prone to skin trauma. They often result from pimples, insect bites, scratching, burns, or other injuries. Certain medical procedures, such as surgical incisions or earlobe piercings, are also known to trigger keloid formation. For example, keloids may develop behind the ears following otoplasty (ear surgery). Keloids can occur in individuals of all ages, but they are less common in children under the age of 11, even when they have their ears pierced. Keloids may also develop as a result of pseudofolliculitis barbae (razor bumps). Continued shaving in the presence of razor bumps can irritate the skin, leading to infection and eventual keloid formation. Men with razor bumps are advised to stop shaving temporarily to allow the skin to heal before resuming hair removal. Diagnosis of keloids is primarily based on physical examination. They are often identified by their characteristic appearance and location on the body. Treatment options for keloids vary in effectiveness, and no single method is considered 100% effective. Surgical removal of keloids requires meticulous care, as recurrence rates are high—approximately 50%. Keloids that recur after excision may grow larger than the original lesion. Combining surgery with other treatments, such as corticosteroid injections, can reduce the likelihood of recurrence. Techniques like V-plasty or W-plasty, which minimize skin tension during wound closure, are also effective in reducing recurrence rates. Silicone gel dressings or moist wound coverings have been shown to reduce the prominence of keloids over time. This treatment is safe and painless, though some patients may experience increased itching with prolonged use. Steroid injections, such as triamcinolone acetonide, can reduce the size and irritation of keloids. These injections are most effective when administered early in the scar's development. However, the procedure can be uncomfortable, particularly for large or hard scars, and may require local or general anesthesia depending on the patient's age. Compression therapy, involving the application of pressure bandages for several months, can lead to a reduction in keloid size. This method is particularly effective in preventing the formation of new scars. Cryosurgery, which involves freezing the keloid tissue, is effective for small keloids on lightly pigmented skin. It is often combined with monthly corticosteroid injections. However, cryotherapy can cause skin blanching and is limited in its application. Radiation therapy, such as electron beam or orthovoltage radiation, can reduce scar formation when used shortly after surgery while the wound is still healing. This is one of the most effective treatments for keloids. Laser therapy is an alternative to conventional surgery for keloid removal. While lasers can produce a superficial peel, they are less effective at reducing the bulk of the keloid. Dye-tuned lasers have not demonstrated superior results compared to cold lasers. Emerging treatments, including drugs used for autoimmune diseases or cancer, such as alpha-interferon, 5-fluorouracil, and bleomycin, have shown promise. However, further research and evaluation are needed to establish their efficacy. A case presentation involves a young male with bilateral keloid formation on the plantar surfaces of both feet. He has not received prior treatment for this condition. Additionally, smaller keloids are present on hairless areas of the skin.
